title: Rep. Omar gives 'strange' response when asked once more if she's related to her ex-husband in first interview since D.C. raid
text:
MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA – AUGUST 8: U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) speaks during a get out the vote event with Democratic Senate candidate, Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, at Cedar Field Park on August 8, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Flanagan and Rep. Angie Craig (D-MN) will be vying for the Democratic nomination in the state’s August 11 primary election. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) OAN Staff Brooke Mallory and Lillian Mann
8:15 PM – Thursday, October 22, 2026
Minnesota Democrat Representative Ilhan Omar sparked wide commentary following her strange and slightly concerning response during her first interview since federal law enforcement agents executed a search warrant at her Washington residence.
Speaking with Chris Hayes on MS NOW , the Minnesota Democrat addressed long-standing claims that she was related to her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.
When asked directly if there was any truth to claims that she had been married to a relative, Omar answered, “Not to my knowledge,” before later calling the accusations baseless. Her choice of words drew immediate attention and criticism online, with political commentators describing the phrasing as surprisingly evasive for a straightforward question regarding her family background.
During the interview, Omar attempted to clarify the origins of the rumors, attributing them to “fringe” Somali blogs and right-wing politicians who she claimed “fabricated narratives” to undermine her political career.
She also dismissed reports that she had previously introduced Elmi to acquaintances as her brother, calling such statements absurd. Omar insisted that these recurring stories are part of a years-long “smear campaign” intended to create sensational headlines. Nonetheless, critics were still quick to point out that replying “not to my knowledge” to a question about sibling relationship status raised serious doubt rather than putting the rumors and controversy to rest.
The television appearance comes in the wake of an October 12 th federal search executed by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) at her Washington home. Omar recounted her initial shock during the morning raid, describing how agents conducted a thorough room-by-room search and seized 17 items, including electronic devices, notebooks, a camera and a language book.
While describing the search as intrusive, she admitted that the agents acted professionally and left the premises in order. The congresswoman argued that she has done nothing wrong, labeling the ongoing Department of Justice investigation once more as a politically motivated effort orchestrated by her opponents to intimidate her ahead of elections.
The federal investigation reportedly centers on allegations of immigration fraud, examining historical documentation connected to naturalization records. Despite Omar’s efforts to pivot the focus back to what she refers to as “political persecution,” her unusual wording during the broadcast has kept the scrutiny surrounding her past personal relationships in the media spotlight.
Meanwhile, this also follows ongoing public scrutiny regarding discrepancies in her historical documentation and official name filings. Recent media reports have highlighted that “Omar'” is not be her primary birth surname, pointing to records that match the last name of her ex-husband, and alleged brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.
According to two people familiar with the investigation, her actual name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. If proven in court that Omar has lived her “entire life under an alias,” a former Minnesota federal immigration judge told Fox News Digital that every single form she ever filled out could be “called into question.”
Additionally, if Omar used an alternate name or incorrect birth date on immigration documents, passport renewals or other official records over the past decade, she could face legal charges.
On Wednesday, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro filed a motion to keep the federal search warrant for the congresswoman’s home sealed. In response to requests from several news organizations to release the document, the motion argues that the federal government is still executing the warrant and that unsealing it now would be premature.
Questions surrounding the congresswoman’s immigration history date back to her first campaign for the Minnesota state House in 2016, leading to an initial federal inquiry during the first Trump administration.
Nonetheless, under the second Trump administration, scrutiny has renewed over allegations that the representative for Minnesota’s 5 th Congressional District in the U.S. House provided false birth information on official forms during naturalization or that she married her brother in 2009 to help him apply for a green card.
